blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — surgical-smoke engineering control and occupational exposure prevention
stem: During electrosurgery, why should local surgical-smoke evacuation remain active whenever smoke is produced?

options.A: To capture plume-generated airborne contaminants close to the surgical source before they disperse into the room.
options.B: To increase general room air exchange after the plume disperses so staff exposure can be reduced through dilution.
options.C: To prevent the electrosurgical generator from causing electromagnetic interference with physiologic monitoring equipment.
options.D: To replace other exposure-control measures during electrosurgery once the smoke evacuator is operating near the surgical site.

rationale: A is correct. NIOSH states that electrosurgical smoke may contain hazardous gases, vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses, and that general room ventilation alone is not sufficient to capture contaminants generated at the source. Local exhaust ventilation such as a smoke evacuator should capture the plume close to the surgical site and remain activated when airborne particles are produced. B incorrectly describes post-dispersion general dilution rather than source capture. C is unrelated to smoke control. D incorrectly treats local evacuation as a replacement for other exposure-control measures.
educational_objective: Use local surgical-smoke evacuation during electrosurgical plume generation to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse into the room.

option_audit.A: Correct; describes local source capture before plume dispersal.
option_audit.B: Plausible ventilation concept but incorrect because local smoke evacuation is intended to capture contaminants near the source, not merely dilute them after room dispersion.
option_audit.C: Plausible electrosurgical technical concern but unrelated to smoke evacuation's occupational-hazard function.
option_audit.D: Plausible overgeneralization but incorrect because engineering control does not replace the broader hierarchy of exposure controls.
